title: Hard exam 4
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: patterns that expand too early, counts that are not what they seem, inverted loop conditions, redirections that run without privileges and background groups.

questions.title: Expanding in two steps
questions.text: `a.txt` and `b.txt` are the only files in the directory. What does `f='*.txt'; echo $f; echo "$f"; echo '$f'` print?

options.t: `a.txt b.txt`, `a.txt b.txt` and `$f`
options.why: Double quotes stop the pattern expansion as well, not only the splitting.

options.t: `*.txt`, `*.txt` and `$f`
options.why: Assigning the value does not keep the star from the pattern expansion of the unquoted `echo $f`.

options.t: `a.txt b.txt`, `*.txt` and `*.txt`
options.why: Single quotes block the variable too, so the third word is `$f`.

options.t: `a.txt b.txt`, `*.txt` and `$f`
options.why: The unquoted `$f` is replaced and then its pattern is expanded; the double quotes keep the text of the variable; the single quotes keep `$f` itself.

questions.title: Names of the files
questions.text: A student wants to print just the names of the `.log` files that contain the word `error`, and runs `grep -c error *.log`. With `a.log` having two matching lines and `b.log` none, what is wrong?

options.t: Nothing is wrong: the output is just the name `a.log`, the only file with matches.
options.why: `-c` does not select files; it prints a count.

options.t: It prints `a.log:2` and `b.log:0`: a count per file, even without matches.
options.why: `-l` is the option that lists only the names of files that contain a match.

options.t: It prints the two matching lines of `a.log`, because `-c` stands for "contents".
options.why: `-c` means count.

options.t: It fails, because `-c` cannot be used with several files.
options.why: With several files it prefixes each count with the file name.

questions.title: The unquoted pattern
questions.text: The current directory has `a.txt` and `c.txt`, and a subdirectory `sub` with `b.txt`. What happens with `find . -name *.txt`, written without quotes?

options.t: It lists `./a.txt`, `./c.txt` and `./sub/b.txt`.
options.why: The shell expands `*.txt` before `find` runs, so `find` does not receive the pattern.

options.t: It lists only `./a.txt` and `./c.txt`, the files of the current directory.
options.why: `-name` would then get two arguments: that is not what happens.

options.t: It fails: `find . -name a.txt c.txt` has an extra path after the expression.
options.why: With two matches in the current directory the shell passes two names, and `find` complains that paths must precede the expression.

options.t: It lists only `./sub/b.txt`, because the other two files were already expanded.
options.why: Expansion does not remove files from the search.

questions.title: Counting without a final newline
questions.text: `nf` was created with `printf 'one two\nthree'`, so its last line has no newline at the end. What does `wc -l -w -c nf` report for lines, words and bytes?

options.why: `wc -l` counts newline characters, and there is only one; and the file has 13 bytes, not 14.
`-l` counts newline characters, not lines of text: the last line is not terminated.
One newline, three words (`one`, `two`, `three`) and 13 bytes (7 + 1 + 5).
`one two` is two words, and `three` is a third one.

questions.title: A countdown that never counts
questions.text:
This script should print `3`, `2`, `1` and stop:
```
n=3
while [ $n -eq 0 ]
do echo $n; n=$((n-1))
done
```
What is wrong?

options.t: It runs forever, because `n` is never compared with 3.
options.why: It does not even enter the loop.

options.t: It prints `3`, `2`, `1` and `0`, because the test is made after the body.
options.why: `while` tests before the body.

options.t: It is a syntax error: `do` must be on the same line as `while`.
options.why: The layout is valid; a newline can precede `do`.

options.t: The condition is inverted: the loop runs only while `n` equals 0, so the body never runs.
options.why: It needs `[ $n -ne 0 ]` with `while`, or `until [ $n -eq 0 ]`.

questions.title: Distinct colours
questions.text:
What does this print?
```
printf 'Red
red
BLUE
blue
red
' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort -u | wc -l
```

options.why: `sort -u` removes the repeated lines before `wc` counts them.
That would be the result without the `tr`: `Red`, `red`, `BLUE` and `blue` are four different lines.
`tr` turns everything into lower case, so there are only `red` and `blue`; `sort -u` keeps one of each.
There are only two different words once the case is the same.

questions.title: What gzip leaves
questions.text: `report.txt` exists. You run `gzip report.txt` and then `ls`. What does `ls` show?

options.t: `report.txt` and `report.txt.gz`
options.why: `gzip` replaces the file with its compressed version unless it is told to keep the original.

options.t: Only `report.txt.gz`
options.why: The compressed file takes the place of the original; `gunzip` would restore `report.txt` and remove the `.gz`.

options.t: Only `report.txt`, because `gzip` compresses in place and keeps the name.
options.why: The result has the extension `.gz`.

options.t: `report.tgz`, as `gzip` always archives and compresses.
options.why: `.tgz` is what `tar` with `z` creates; `gzip` only compresses one file.

questions.title: Execute only for the others
questions.text: `ls -ld dd` shows `drwxr-x--x 2 ana dev 4096 Mar 3 10:00 dd`, and `dd/f` has mode `rw-r--r--`. A user who is neither ana nor in `dev` runs `ls dd` and then `cat dd/f`. What happens?

options.t: Both work, because `f` is readable by everybody.
options.why: Listing the directory needs `r` on it, which the others do not have.

options.t: Both fail, because the others have no `r` on the directory.
options.why: Reading `f` through the path only needs `x` on the directory.

options.t: `ls dd` fails with `Permission denied`, but `cat dd/f` prints the file.
options.why: `x` allows traversing the directory to a name that is already known; without `r` the names cannot be listed.

options.t: `ls dd` works, but `cat dd/f` fails, because `x` on a directory means execute.
options.why: It is the other way round: `x` allows crossing it and `r` is what lists it.

questions.title: sudo and the redirection
questions.text: A normal user, who is allowed to use `sudo`, runs `sudo echo hi > /etc/zz`. What happens?

options.t: The file `/etc/zz` is created containing `hi`, because `sudo` gives root rights to the whole line.
options.why: `sudo` only affects the command that follows it, `echo`.

options.t: The shell reports `Permission denied`, because the redirection is done by the user's shell, not by root.
options.why: `echo` is not the problem: the `> /etc/zz` is opened by the shell before `sudo` runs; `echo hi | sudo tee /etc/zz` would work.

options.t: `sudo` asks for the password and then writes the file.
options.why: The failure happens before `sudo` has a chance to write anything.

options.t: The text `hi` is printed on the screen and the file is created empty.
options.why: The file cannot be created at all by a normal user.

questions.title: Background of a group
questions.text: You run `(sleep 2; echo A) & echo B` at the prompt. What do you see?

options.t: `A` after two seconds, and then `B`.
options.why: `echo B` is not part of the group that was sent to the background.

options.t: Only `B`, because the background group is killed when the line ends.
options.why: A background group goes on running, and prints its output when it finishes.

options.t: `B` at once, and `A` about two seconds later.
options.why: The `&` applies to the parenthesised group only; the shell continues with `echo B` immediately.

options.t: `A` and `B` at once, because `sleep` is not waited for when it runs in a group.
options.why: The `sleep` happens inside the group, before its `echo A`, which comes two seconds later.
